key_concept: For a non-relativistic electron $p_e=\sqrt{2mE}$, while for a photon $p_{Ph}=\frac{E}{c}$, so $\frac{p_e}{p_{Ph}}=c\sqrt{\frac{2m}{E}}$.
steps: The question statement has a misprint. The mass of the electron is simply $m=9\times10^{-31}$ kg; the $\frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}$ is irrelevant here.
Convert the energy to joules: $E=20\text{ eV}=20\times1.6\times10^{-19}=3.2\times10^{-18}$ J.
The electron's kinetic energy (20 eV) is far below its rest energy (about 0.5 MeV), so it is non-relativistic. Hence $p_e=\sqrt{2mE}$.
why_not_others: Options (1) and (2) are less than 1, which would mean the photon has more momentum than the electron. That happens only if the ratio is inverted ($\frac{p_{Ph}}{p_e}=\frac{1}{225}$) or the formulas are swapped. Option (4) comes from an arithmetic slip.
common_trap: Using $p=\frac{E}{c}$ for the electron as well, or $p=\sqrt{2mE}$ for the photon, which wrongly gives a ratio of 1 or a meaningless value.
time_saving_tip: Remember $\frac{p_e}{p_{Ph}}=c\sqrt{\frac{2m}{E}}=\sqrt{\frac{2mc^2}{E}}$. With $mc^2\approx\frac{81\times10^{-15}}{1.6\times10^{-19}}\text{ eV}\approx5.06\times10^5$ eV, the ratio is $\sqrt{\frac{2\times5.06\times10^{5}}{20}}=\sqrt{50625}=225$.
